blocks.title: Funding timing
blocks.sub: spending ahead of the next round

blocks.text: Sendy raised its $20M Series B in January 2020, weeks before COVID-19 reached Kenya, then expanded across countries and into fulfilment and supply through the 2021 funding peak. The plan relied on a $100M round in 2022, just as venture markets turned; when it did not close, Sendy was carrying a cost base sized for capital it had not raised. That mismatch, more than any single instrument, is the clearest capital-strategy lesson from the case.

blocks.title: Instrument choice
blocks.sub: equity funded a shift toward assets

blocks.text: Sendy’s original transport business was asset-light: an app coordinating contract drivers who owned their vehicles (Today Africa, n.d.). The capital intensity came later, with warehousing and fulfilment, which carry fixed costs, and a supply business that bought and held retail stock. These lines need working capital and physical assets, which M-KOPA and MNT-Halan fund with debt. Sendy funded them with venture equity, the most expensive capital available, on which a thin-margin logistics business struggles to earn venture returns. Asset-finance or working-capital facilities might have let equity fund the platform alone, but it is not clear such facilities were available on workable terms to a loss-making logistics company in 2021–2022. The lesson is less that Sendy chose the wrong instrument than that it took on asset-intensive lines without a financing route suited to them. Sendy itself exited Nigerian operations as part of a reported shift away from an asset-heavy model (TechCabal, August 2023).

blocks.title: Investor selection
blocks.sub: a strategic investor is not a backstop

blocks.text: Toyota Tsusho’s participation brought credibility, industry relationships and a market signal, but no public commitment to fund Sendy through a downturn. When the $100M round failed and an investor later withdrew, existing shareholders did not close the gap. A strategic investor’s backing is not a guarantee of future support.

blocks.title: Dilution, follow-on funding and decline or delay decisions

blocks.text: Sendy’s attempt to raise at a $40–60M valuation in 2023, against an earlier valuation above $80M, shows how quickly bargaining power erodes when a company raises to survive. With hindsight, one alternative was to delay expansion and focus on Kenyan B2B transport, its most established line; whether that line was profitable on its own is not public. Instead, Sendy ran three product lines in four countries on about $26.5M of disclosed funding.

why: Sendy is this study’s cautionary case. One of Kenya’s best-known logistics startups, with a Japanese strategic investor and multi-country operations, it closed in 2023 after a planned $100M round failed. Its founders built a credible operation. The available evidence suggests its capital strategy contributed to the outcome: the company committed to expansion before the capital was in hand, and moved from an asset-light transport marketplace into fulfilment and supply lines that required fixed costs and working capital, funded with equity. Operating costs, customer pricing and the 2022–2023 funding downturn also played a part (The Star, August 2023).
lessons: Never size the cost base to capital you have not raised; Sendy’s expansion assumed a $100M round that had not closed.

Match the financing route to the asset before adding asset-intensive lines: warehouses, inventory and working capital need asset or working-capital finance, or a partner who carries them, rather than venture equity.
A strategic investor brings credibility, not a commitment to fund the next round.

facts.business: On-demand delivery, then B2B transport, fulfilment and supply
facts.investors: Safaricom’s Spark Fund, Atlantica Ventures, Toyota Tsusho
facts.status: Ceased operations Aug 2023; administrator appointed Sept 2023

entries.text: Commercial launch in Kenya as an on-demand delivery app. Investment from Safaricom’s Spark Fund.
KES 207.6M (about $2M) equity investment from DOB Equity and CFAO Group, a Toyota Tsusho subsidiary, described by the CEO as growth capital (Business Daily, November 2017).
$2M equity investment from Goodwell Investments (Ventureburn, October 2019).
$20M Series B led by Atlantica Ventures, with Toyota Tsusho Corporation participating (Today Africa, n.d.).

Launches Sendy Fulfilment (warehousing) and Sendy Supply (retail sourcing); expands into Uganda and Nigeria, and takes a minority stake in Côte d’Ivoire’s Kamtar with Toyota Tsusho’s Mobility 54 (Business Daily, October 2021). Seeks $100M to fund pan-African expansion; the round does not close, beyond a small investment from MOL PLUS. Lays off 10% of staff in July 2022; Sendy Supply shuts in October 2022 with a further 10% cut, and Transport becomes B2B only (Techpoint Africa, August 2023).

Suspends on-the-ground operations in Nigeria in February. A key investor withdraws, and talks with new investors depend on a valuation of $40–60M, against an earlier valuation above $80M. Operations cease in August; an administrator is appointed in September (The Star, August 2023; Today Africa, n.d.).
